A1.justification: Both PDFs describe JOWA and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–F. Retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Atari pretraining, model-scaling, held-out-game fine-tuning, and ablation results in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds FICC and MCTS comparisons, smaller-model transfer results, non-expert-data fine-tuning, and a Zaxxon analysis.

M1.justification: The shared transformer, VQ-VAE, world-model and distributional CQL objectives, two-stage pretraining, and beam-search planner remain unchanged. MCTS is an evaluated alternative. Omitting parts of the fine-tuning recipe does not establish that the underlying procedure changed.

E1.justification: The DQN-Replay dataset and the same 15 pretraining and five held-out games are retained. Appendix F adds transfer scenarios using suboptimal and highly suboptimal demonstrations, extending the previously expert-only fine-tuning coverage to poorer-quality inputs.

E2.justification: v3 adds an offline-adapted FICC-85M comparator to both pretraining and transfer comparisons in Tables 2–3. It also evaluates adapted MuZero-style MCTS against JOWA's planner and no planning in Tables 5 and 19. These substantially extend comparisons with alternative model-based approaches.

E3.justification: Reported fine-tuning budgets increase from 10k to 50k steps, and scratch training from 100k to 500k, despite retained scores. This establishes changed reported settings, not that experiments were rerun. New protocols cover FICC adaptation, smaller-model transfer, MCTS tuning and FPS measurement, demonstration-quality sampling, and reward-clipped Zaxxon evaluation.

E4.justification: v3 adds planning-quality and speed comparisons with MCTS, transfer sensitivity to demonstration quality, and a Zaxxon case study testing whether apparent emergence reflects nonlinear rewards. Existing loss, synthetic-data, Q-head ensemble, and task-embedding ablations remain; the latter two discussions move to Appendix F.

E5.justification: Both versions specify averaging each game score over 16 rollout episodes in Appendix E.3. No new training-seed reporting, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests are introduced. Zaxxon reward-event counts add outcomes, not a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: New results include FICC's 0.433 pretraining IQM HNS and 0.575 transfer IQM DNS, plus transfer IQM DNS of 0.498 and 0.603 for JOWA-40M and 70M. Table 5 reports planner/MCTS FPS of 1.26/0.12 and mean HNS of 37.8%/22.1%. Table 21 adds mean DNS of 0.516 and 0.422 for poorer-quality data. Retained pretraining, transfer, and ablation scores are unchanged; revised transfer budgets prevent interpreting them as same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: v3 removes the explicit COMBO objective and accompanying definition of the real/synthetic-data mixture from v1 Section 3.2. The paper's own Theorem 4.1, formal assumptions, and derivations and proofs in Appendices A–C remain unchanged apart from numbering and wording.

C1.justification: The joint-optimization, scaling, and sample-efficient-transfer contributions remain. The headline pretraining advantage changes from 31.6% to 71.4% while JOWA's score stays 0.789: the tables support a shift from percentage-point gaps to relative gains with FICC included. The introduction also adds a 69.9% transfer-advantage claim without clearly specifying its averaging calculation.

C2.justification: v3 adds qualifications that aggregate scaling can coexist with declining individual-game scores and that transfer depends on demonstration quality. Appendix F attributes apparent Zaxxon emergence to nonlinear rewards and discusses MCTS sensitivity, including unsuccessful tuning on eight other games. The original joint-optimization and synthetic-data interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v3 documents FICC adaptation, MCTS implementation and tuning, and selection of the final pretraining checkpoint. However, it removes explicit fine-tuning unfreezing instructions, stage allocation, the 3:1 real/synthetic batch mixture, and the COMBO-loss specification, plus exact parameter counts. Most architecture and optimizer tables remain. The same repository URL and future-release statements do not establish newly available resources.

R1.justification: v3 adds positioning against FICC and references supporting the MCTS and emergence discussions, alongside Genie and newer RL citations. It prunes numerous broad introductory and related-work references. Table 1 replaces MTDIFF with FICC, although MTDIFF's cited work remains elsewhere. The central positioning around scalable, jointly optimized offline model-based RL is retained.

P1.justification: v3 shortens introductory and background passages, creates a dedicated baseline subsection, moves ensemble and task-embedding discussions to Appendix F, and updates author information and the conference header. These are localized revisions; most methodological exposition and the overall narrative structure remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The principal comparison tables expand with FICC and smaller-model transfer columns. New displays present planning speed/performance, raw planning scores, and data-quality results. The main ablation table is narrowed while its complete results remain in the appendix, and several hyperparameter tables are rearranged. Figures 1–2 retain their substantive content.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens empirical support through a relevant model-based comparator, an explicit planning comparison, and tests qualifying transfer and scaling claims. These provide useful evidence beyond v1's retained headline results. The gain is limited by removal of important fine-tuning instructions and an unexplained fivefold budget revision accompanying unchanged legacy scores; new transfer entries also lack corresponding per-game results in Table 18.
